newsitem.title: FRANCE: Alcatel keeps mum on GEC Alsthom intentions. [CORRECTED 15:22 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Alcatel keeps mum on GEC Alsthom intentions. [CORRECTED 15:22 GMT]

text.p: French engineering and telecoms group Alcatel Alsthom kept mum on Monday about its intentions concerning GEC Alsthom amid rumours that General Electric Co Plc may bail out.

GEC chief executive George Simpson will unveil his strategy for the British group on Tuesday and analysts expect him to concentrate on defence and exit both the GPT joint venture with Siemens and GEC Alsthom.
GEC Alsthom, which makes industrial power plants and high-speed trains, is 50-50 owned by the French and British groups and both are uncomfortable with the situation.
"(Alcatel chairman Serge) Tchuruk told the shareholders meeting (on June 19) that he was dissatisfied with the current situation at GEC Alsthom," said an Alcatel spokesman.
He added that Tchuruk had confirmed that there were "contacts" with the British group.
In March, presenting the annual results, Tchuruk told a news conference there were talks with GEC which went beyond the joint-venture.
Ever since Tchuruk took the helm at Alcatel in June 1995, he has made it clear that he did not like the group's many joint-ventures in which the issue of control was not resolved.
Soon thereafter the French engineering company renewed its bid to obtain a majority stake in state-controlled nuclear energy group Framatome.
Alcatel has a 44 percent stake in Framatome and was planning to merge Framatome with GEC Alsthom in a move which would have given the French group a bigger stake in GEC Alsthom Framatome than GEC.

Tchuruk foresaw a separate Bourse listing for GEC Alsthom in the future, at which time both Alcatel and GEC could reduce their stakes in the company while GEC Alsthom's management -- led by Pierre Bilger -- would focus on financial results for the share market.

But this plan was abandoned as talks failed in April. GEC's Simpson did not want less than 50 percent of the enlarged group while the French government wanted French interests -- including Alcatel -- to keep a majority in the large venture.
Since then it has been quiet around GEC Alsthom. It has won contracts here and there, such as a 465 million franc order for an electricity plant in Argentina last month.
But it could do with more size and spread to better compete with Asea Brown Boveri, Siemens, Westinghouse Electric Corp or General Electric (GE) of the United States.

GEC Alsthom NV had 1996 sales of 59.8 billion francs, new orders of 59.4 billion, operating profit of 2.8 billion, and employed 83,000 people at the end of last year. (Corrects by doubling sales, orders and staff figures given in Alcatel annual report to give GEC Alsthom totals.)
It is the world's number two in engineering for transport and distribution of energy, number two in rail transport and number three in energy production.
Established in 1988, it has been incorporated in the Netherlands since 1989, benefitting from certain tax advantages.
GEC Alsthom is not the only subject of joint interest for the French and British groups. GEC has declared its interest in obtaining a stake in French defence group Thomson-CSF.

The new Socialist-led government has not yet unveiled its strategy concerning the state's 58 percent stake in Thomson-CSF. The previous government was considering bids from Lagardere Groupe and a joint offer from Alcatel and Dassault Aviation.
